name: Web 1.0 vernacular (GeoCities)
plain: Homemade 90s web page: tiled backgrounds, blinking GIFs, everything at once.
origin: Amateur personal home pages of the mid 1990s, hosted on services like GeoCities (1994 to 2009) [S1][S3]
defining: Repeating tiled backgrounds, very often starry outer space, behind everything [S2]
Animated GIFs everywhere: 'Under Construction' signs, blinking yellow 'New!' buttons, glitter text later on [S2]
Background MIDI music and collections of ready-made web graphics [S2]
No clear structure: blocks of graphics and text dropped on a background, pages left permanently under construction [S2][S3]
Browser-default type and colours (serif body text, blue underlined links) [inferred]
code: body{background:#000 url(stars.gif) repeat;color:#ff0;font-family:'Times New Roman',serif} a{color:#0ff} /* [inferred] values */
fits: Fan pages, personal sites, zines, playful portfolios and nostalgic campaigns.
goes_wrong: Pastiche without content: moving GIFs and clashing colours bury the message and slow the page.
accessibility: Blinking GIFs and busy tiled backgrounds hurt reading and can trigger seizures; keep text on a solid panel at 4.5:1, never flash more than 3 times a second, and stop animation under prefers-reduced-motion.

sources.supports: Olia Lialina's essay: the mid-90s amateur web was bright, personal, slow and under construction
Under Construction signs, outer space and starry backgrounds, MIDI files, blinking New! buttons, glitter graphics, repeating backgrounds, no clear structure
GeoCities hosted personal homepages 1994 to 2009, over 38 million pages; spaces were expected to be always under construction

examples.name: Cameron's World
examples.what: A web collage of text and images taken from archived GeoCities pages

examples.name: Neocities
examples.what: A free host for handmade personal static sites, in the GeoCities spirit, since 2013

name: Classic Mac (1-bit System software)
plain: Black and white early Mac screen: striped title bars, tiny pixel fonts.
origin: Apple Macintosh System software, 1984 to 1991; System 6 was the last monochrome version [S1]
defining: Pure black and white pixels only; tone comes from dither patterns such as checkerboards [S2][S3]
Window title bars filled with thin horizontal black stripes [S3]
Rounded-rectangle buttons about 59 x 20 px; dialogs with a 2px border and a 2px hard offset shadow [S1][S3]
Bitmap system fonts: Chicago for menus and titles, Geneva for small text, Monaco for code [S3]
Differs from pixel-art: this is window chrome and controls, not illustration [inferred]
fits: Writing apps, indie tools, retro games, nostalgic product pages and personal sites.
goes_wrong: Tiny bitmap type and dense dither patterns at modern screen sizes become hard to read and feel like a costume.
accessibility: Black on white passes easily, but dither patterns behind text fail; keep text on solid white, scale bitmap fonts in whole multiples, and add a clear focus outline.

sources.supports: Recreates Apple System software 1984 to 1991, based on System 6 as the last monochrome version; standard button 59 x 20 px, buttons are rounded rectangles
Susan Kare drew the first Mac icons with basic black-and-white pixels, one graph-paper box per pixel; sketches acquired by MoMA
Stylesheet values: striped title bar gradient, 2px dialog border and 2px offset shadow, checkerboard pattern, Chicago, Geneva and Monaco fonts

examples.name: system.css
examples.what: A CSS library that rebuilds System 6 windows, buttons and menus

name: Windows 95 classic
plain: Grey 90s PC windows with raised buttons and a blue title bar.
origin: Microsoft Windows 95 (1995); the bevelled 3D look was popularised earlier by NeXTSTEP and OS/2 2.0 [S1]
defining: Silver grey (#c0c0c0) windows and buttons [S2]
Raised bevels from stacked 1px inset shadows: white and light grey top-left, grey and near-black bottom-right; pressed buttons flip to sunken [S2]
Navy title bar, fading to a lighter blue in the Windows 98 version [S2]
Small pixel-style sans type; buttons at least 75 x 23 px [S2]
A taskbar with one Start button as the home base for every task [S3]
fits: Retro games, developer and internal tools with a wink, playful portfolios, nostalgia campaigns.
goes_wrong: Rebuilding a whole fake desktop inside a web page so real navigation hides behind toy windows.
accessibility: Bevels are the only state cue; keep near-black text on silver (well above 4.5:1), add a visible focus outline, and do not rely on a 1px bevel alone to tell pressed from disabled.

sources.supports: Windows 95 controls, dialogs and menus have a bevelled 3D look popularised by NeXTSTEP and OS/2 2.0; single Start button
98.css: silver surfaces, inset-shadow bevels, raised borders become sunken when pressed, navy to blue title bar, 75 x 23 px minimum buttons, pixel MS Sans Serif
Kent Sullivan's Microsoft usability paper: Start menu as a single-button home base, taskbar for switching windows

examples.name: 98.css
examples.what: A semantic, accessible CSS library that recreates Windows 98 controls

name: Mac OS Platinum
plain: Soft grey late-90s Mac windows with gentle 3D buttons.
origin: Apple Mac OS 8 and 9, first built for the cancelled Copland system [S4]
defining: Many shades of light grey, replacing the mostly black and white System 7 look, as a system-wide appearance people could switch off [S1][S4]
Bevel buttons are a standard control next to push buttons, radio buttons and checkboxes [S3]
People pick accent and highlight colours, used for selections, progress bars and scroll thumbs [S2][S4]
Charcoal as the system font, with Chicago as an option [S4]
Keeps System 7 shapes and positions; only the rendering turned grey and 3D [S4]
fits: Retro creative tools, music apps, calm utilities and nostalgic Apple-flavoured portfolios.
goes_wrong: Grey on grey with faint bevels makes every control look disabled.
accessibility: Light grey surfaces cut contrast; keep text near black (4.5:1 or more on the grey), give controls a 3:1 edge, and show focus with an outline, not only the accent colour.

sources.supports: Apple Mac OS 8 Human Interface Guidelines: system-wide platinum appearance that people can switch on or off
Same guidelines: figures use platinum appearance; the Appearance control panel offers a range of accent and highlight colours
Same guidelines: controls chapter lists push buttons, radio buttons, checkboxes and bevel buttons
Platinum was meant for Copland; shades of grey replace black and white; Charcoal default font with Chicago option; palettes for progress bars, scroll thumbs and selections

examples.name: Classicy
examples.what: React components replicating Mac OS 8 interface parts, including bevel buttons and Platinum list views

name: Aqua (early Mac OS X)
plain: Shiny blue gel buttons, pinstriped windows and soft shadows.
origin: Apple Mac OS X, unveiled at Macworld San Francisco in January 2000 [S1]
defining: Luminous, semi-transparent buttons, scroll bars and windows with fluid animation [S1]
Blue, white and grey palette; the default button is blue and pulses [S2]
Gel or glass highlight on rounded controls; red, yellow and green window buttons [S2]
Early window backgrounds use fine pinstripes, later plain white; windows are separated by drop shadows, not frames [S2]
Lucida Grande system type; windows shrink into the Dock with the Genie effect [S2]
fits: Media players, playful utilities, nostalgic product pages and early-2000s tributes.
goes_wrong: Gloss on everything: when every control shines, nothing reads as the main action.
accessibility: White text on mid-blue gel can fall below 4.5:1; use dark text on light gel or deepen the blue, and stop pulsing buttons under prefers-reduced-motion.

sources.supports: Apple press release, 5 January 2000: Aqua has luminous, semi-transparent buttons, scroll bars and windows and fluid animation
Blue, white and grey palette, gel effect, pulsing default button, pinstripes then white, drop shadows, Lucida Grande, Genie effect, graphite option

name: Windows XP Luna
plain: Bright blue rounded title bars, green Start button, beige windows.
origin: Microsoft Windows XP (2001), visual style developed with Frog Design [S2]
defining: Saturated blue title bars with a glossy vertical gradient and about 8px rounded top corners [S1][S2]
Warm beige-grey window body (#ece9d8); buttons with a 3px radius, dark blue border and white-to-beige gradient [S1]
Trebuchet MS for title bars, Tahoma for most other text [S2]
Shipped in blue, olive green and silver; critics called it a Fisher-Price interface [S2]
Differs from frutiger-aero: opaque plastic chrome, not glass, water or nature imagery [inferred]
fits: Nostalgia sites, retro game interfaces, playful dashboards and 2000s-themed campaigns.
goes_wrong: Heavy saturated chrome competes with content and reads as childish in serious products.
accessibility: White title text on the light end of the blue gradient can dip below 4.5:1; deepen the gradient or add a dark text shadow, and keep focus outlines visible on beige.

sources.supports: XP.css stylesheet: title bar blue gradient, 8px top radius, Trebuchet MS title, #ece9d8 body, 3px button radius with gradient
Luna by Frog Design, saturated colours and rounded window corners, blue, olive green and silver variants, Trebuchet MS and Tahoma, Fisher-Price nickname

examples.name: XP.css
examples.what: A CSS library extending 98.css with Windows XP windows, buttons and title bars

name: Web 2.0 gloss
plain: Shiny buttons, reflections, big friendly text and a 'Free!' starburst.
origin: Web-app and startup sites from the mid 2000s to the early 2010s [S1][S3]
defining: Bright saturated colours, green the unofficial favourite, plus blues, oranges and pinks [S1]
Rounded corners on everything and rounded typefaces in logos [S1]
Big text, short copy, white space and starburst badges shouting Free or Beta [S1][S2]
Glossy buttons: a two-tone gradient with a hard split near the middle and a white highlight over the top half; mirror reflections under product shots [S3][S2]
Differs from frutiger-aero: a landing-page formula without its sky, water and nature imagery [inferred]
fits: Retro-themed landing pages, playful product launches and nostalgic SaaS tributes.
goes_wrong: The checklist trap: gradient, badge, reflection and huge type added by habit rather than purpose [S2].
accessibility: White text on bright green or orange gloss often fails; test the lightest gradient stop behind text at 4.5:1.

sources.supports: 2006 essay: bright colours with green as the unofficial colour, rounded corners and typefaces, Free starbursts, big text, white space
2008 article: the unwritten Web 2.0 checklist of gradients, round corners, mirror effects, a badge and very large key text
2025 how-to: Web 2.0 Gloss common about 2007 to early 2010s; glossy two-tone gradient button with a top highlight, reflections under objects

examples.name: Frutiger Aero Archive
examples.what: Site built with CSS glossy buttons in the Web 2.0 Gloss manner

name: Metro (Microsoft Design Language)
plain: Flat bright tiles and big thin lowercase words, no decoration.
origin: Microsoft: early signs in Encarta 95, Media Center and Zune, launched as Metro with Windows Phone 7 in 2010 [S1]
defining: Typography first: very large, light headings, often lowercase, on sideways-scrolling canvases [S1]
Flat solid-colour square and wide tiles; live tiles animate fresh content [S1][S3]
No faux textures, shadows, bevels or 3D icons; content before chrome [S2]
Rooted in Swiss graphic design and public transit signage [S1]
Motion acknowledges every tap and transition to make the UI feel alive [S1]
fits: Glanceable status dashboards, media hubs, kiosks, TV and touch-first apps.
goes_wrong: Flat tiles hide what is clickable and spread little information over a lot of space [S3].
accessibility: Flat text links lack affordance and white text on light tile colours can fail; mark actions with icons or underlines, check every tile colour at 4.5:1, and stop live-tile animation under reduced motion.

sources.supports: History from Encarta 95 to Windows Phone 7 (2010), Swiss design and transit-sign roots, light thin font, lowercase headings, large titles, live tiles, motion
Microsoft's Windows Store app principles: authentically digital, bold vibrant colours, beautiful typography, content before chrome
NN/g 2012: flat style reduces discoverability, low information density, overly live tiles backfire

name: Material You / Material 3 Expressive
plain: Soft colour pulled from your wallpaper, chunky rounded shapes, springy motion.
origin: Google: dynamic colour arrived in Android 12; Material 3 Expressive pairs with Android 16 [S1][S2]
defining: One source colour from the wallpaper becomes five key colours, each turned into a 13-tone palette for light and dark schemes [S1]
A shape scale from square to fully round, and polygon shapes that morph into each other in animation [S2][S4]
Spring-based motion: neighbouring items react as you drag and dismiss [S3]
Expressive version uses size, colour, shape and containment to push the key action; 46 studies with 18,000+ people found key elements spotted up to 4x faster [S5]
Differs from material-elevation (Material 1 paper and shadow): depth comes mostly from tonal colour, not drop shadows [inferred]
fits: Android apps, consumer mobile products, personalised dashboards and friendly productivity tools.
goes_wrong: Wallpaper colours mixed by hand give muddy, low-contrast pairs; use the paired on-colour roles instead.
accessibility: Always pair each container colour with its on-colour role to keep 4.5:1, and turn shape morphs and springs off under reduced motion.

sources.supports: Dynamic Color added in Android 12: wallpaper source colour, five key colours, 13-tone palettes, light and dark schemes
Compose implements Material You and Material 3 Expressive, which complements Android 16; shape scale from square to fully circular
Google: Material 3 Expressive builds on Material You with springy animations, notifications that respond to drag, blurred shade, shape-morphing on Wear OS
Graphics-shapes library: rounded polygons and Morph objects for animating between shapes
46 studies, 18,000+ participants; colour, shape, size, motion and containment; key elements found up to four times faster

name: Microsoft Fluent (Acrylic and Mica)
plain: Frosted, slightly grainy panels over a softly tinted Windows backdrop.
origin: Microsoft, announced at Build 2017 (codename Project Neon) as the successor to Metro [S4][S5]
defining: Acrylic recipe: background, blur, exclusion blend, colour tint and a layer of noise; the noise and tint set it apart from plain glassmorphism [S1]
Mica: an opaque base layer tinted once from the desktop wallpaper, falling back to neutral when the window is inactive [S2]
Two-layer layout: Mica base, then a low-opacity content layer or cards on top [S2]
8px radius for windows, flyouts and dialogs; 4px for buttons and in-page items [S3]
Built on light, depth, motion, material and scale; the Reveal hover light on borders has been discontinued [S4][S5]
code: .pane{background:rgba(243,243,243,.7);backdrop-filter:blur(30px) saturate(125%);border-radius:8px} /* [inferred] values; add a faint noise image for acrylic */
fits: Windows apps, productivity and enterprise tools, settings panels and Office-like web apps.
goes_wrong: Acrylic placed edge to edge creates seams and visual noise; it belongs on transient or secondary surfaces [S1].
accessibility: Acrylic turns solid in High Contrast, Battery Saver and with transparency off; mirror that with prefers-reduced-transparency and avoid accent-coloured text on acrylic [S1].

sources.supports: Acrylic recipe (blur, exclusion blend, tint, noise), seams when placed edge to edge, solid fallbacks, no accent text on acrylic
Mica is opaque, samples the wallpaper once, neutral when inactive; base layer plus content layer
Windows 11 corner radii: 8px top-level containers, 4px in-page controls
Fluent announced 2017 with five elements: light, depth, motion, material and scale
Codename Project Neon, revamp of Metro, Reveal highlight discontinued with WinUI 2.6

name: Apple Liquid Glass
plain: Clear floating glass controls that bend light and shine at edges.
origin: Apple, announced 9 June 2025 for iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26, watchOS 26 and tvOS 26 [S1]
defining: Lensing: the glass bends and concentrates light from the content below, where older materials only scattered it (the frosted blur of glassmorphism) [S2]
Highlights from virtual light sources move around the edge on interaction and with device motion; bigger pieces look thicker, with deeper shadows and stronger refraction [S2]
Only for a floating layer of controls and navigation such as tab bars and sidebars, never the content layer [S3]
Two variants: regular (blurs and adjusts luminosity) and clear (very see-through, with a 35% dark dimming layer over bright media) [S3]
Controls nest concentrically in rounded window corners and shrink or morph as you scroll [S1][S2]
code: .bar{border-radius:999px;background:rgba(255,255,255,.12);backdrop-filter:blur(2px) saturate(180%);box-shadow:inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.6),0 8px 24px rgba(0,0,0,.2)} /* [inferred] approximation; real lensing needs an SVG displacement filter */
fits: Media, photo and map apps and immersive consumer apps with rich content behind the controls.
goes_wrong: Clear glass over busy content loses contrast, and controls that animate for no reason distract [S4].
accessibility: Support Reduce Transparency and Increase Contrast (prefers-reduced-transparency, prefers-contrast) with an opaque fallback; dim behind clear glass and check text at 4.5:1 over the worst background [S3][S4].

sources.supports: Apple newsroom, 9 June 2025: translucent material that reflects and refracts surroundings, real-time specular highlights, tab bars shrink on scroll, platforms list
WWDC25 Meet Liquid Glass: lensing bends and concentrates light, highlights layer, thicker material when larger, concentric nesting in window corners
HIG Materials: not in the content layer, use sparingly, regular and clear variants, 35% dimming layer for bright content
NN/g, October 2025: legibility and contrast problems over busy backgrounds, motion for motion's sake

name: visionOS spatial UI
plain: Floating glass windows in your room that light up when looked at.
origin: Apple visionOS for Apple Vision Pro [S1]; visionOS guidance added to Apple's design guidelines in June 2023 [S2]
defining: Windows sit on a fixed glass material that lets light, the room and other content show through [S2][S3]
No separate dark mode: glass adapts to the brightness behind it, and vibrancy keeps text legible [S2]
The system adds highlights, specular reflections and shadows for depth; ornaments float just off a window's edge [S3]
Looking at a control lights it up (hover effect); keep target centres at least 60 pt apart [S4]
Differs from glassmorphism and liquid-glass: whole windows are glass placed at real distances in 3D space [inferred]
fits: Spatial and AR apps, immersive media, 3D product viewers and pages that preview spatial products.
goes_wrong: Pasting a flat-screen layout onto glass: small, crowded targets and opaque panels feel heavy and are hard to aim at with the eyes [S3][S4].
accessibility: Space targets 60 pt apart, avoid repeating patterns that fill the view, use high-legibility vibrancy for text, and give an opaque option for reduced transparency [S4][S2].

sources.supports: visionOS basics: windows, volumes, immersion, passthrough, eyes and hands
visionOS windows use glass; no distinct Dark Mode, glass adapts to luminance; vibrancy for text; visionOS guidance added June 21, 2023
Default window is an upright plane of glass with specular reflections and shadows; ornaments; opaque backgrounds feel heavy
Hover effect on gaze; 16 pt margin or 60 pt between centres; avoid repeating patterns that fill the field of view

name: E-ink / e-paper
plain: Calm black ink on grey-white paper, no glow and no animation.
origin: Electrophoretic ink from E Ink, used in e-readers, shelf labels and calendars [S1][S2]
defining: Reflective with no backlight: black and white particles in tiny capsules, so it reads like print and holds an image with no power [S1][S2]
Slow changes: a full refresh takes about 2 to 4 seconds and flashes, and fast partial refreshes leave ghosting [S2]
So no animation: state changes are hard cuts, with paging instead of smooth scrolling [S2][inferred]
Very few grey levels (one panel gets 4 greys with a slower waveform); colour panels show a handful of inks with grainy dithering [S2]
fits: Reading apps, focus and calm tools, rarely updated dashboards, low-power devices and wellbeing products.
goes_wrong: Faking it with flat light greys and hairlines, which looks washed out rather than inky.
accessibility: Keep near-black on off-white well above 4.5:1, use thick strokes and large type, and give focus a heavy outline; the lack of motion already suits reduced motion.

sources.supports: E Ink: electronic ink of microcapsules holding white and black charged particles, used to make ePaper displays

Waveshare docs: bistable and reflective, no backlight, full refresh about 2 to 4 s with flashing, ghosting after partial refresh, not suitable for animation, 4-grey mode, Spectra 6 colours with dithering

name: DOS text-mode TUI
plain: Full-screen text windows drawn with line characters on bright blue.
origin: IBM PC programs of the 1980s and early 1990s such as Norton Commander, WordPerfect and Borland's Turbo Vision IDEs (1990) [S1][S2]
defining: Usually a blue background with white or yellow characters [S1]
Frames, windows and dialogs drawn with box-drawing characters from IBM code page 437, such as ┌ and ╣ [S1]
A fixed grid of character cells set in raster text-mode fonts such as IBM VGA 8x16 [S3]
Menu bars, list boxes, check boxes and radio buttons all built from text, with mouse support [S2]
Differs from terminal: a full-screen windowed app made of text, not a scrolling command prompt [inferred]
fits: Developer tools, CLIs with a UI, keyboard-first internal tools, retro games and hacker-themed sites.
goes_wrong: Mixing proportional fonts or fractional widths so the box characters stop lining up.
accessibility: White on deep blue passes, but yellow and cyan accents need checking; make every action keyboard reachable and hide box-drawing art from screen readers.

sources.supports: Blue background with white or yellow characters, box-drawing characters from code page 437, examples Norton Commander, WordPerfect, Turbo Pascal
Borland character-mode framework, 1990, with menus, list boxes, check boxes, radio buttons and mouse support
Archive of DOS-era text-mode raster fonts such as IBM VGA 8x16, free under CC BY-SA 4.0

examples.name: WebTUI
examples.what: A CSS library of terminal-style components with ASCII boxes for the web

examples.name: Turbo Vision (magiblot port)
examples.what: The classic Turbo Vision text UI framework, ported to modern systems

name: CRT phosphor glow
plain: Glowing green or amber letters on black with faint scanlines.
origin: Monochrome CRT monitors of the 1960s to 1980s; P1 phosphor glows green, P3 amber, P4 white [S1]
defining: One colour of light on black: green, amber or 'page white'; emulators keep amber and green presets [S1][S3]
Soft bloom around text, faked with a text-shadow of about 5px [S2]
Horizontal scanlines: a repeating gradient with a 1px dark line every 2px over the content [S2]
A radial glow brightest at the centre of the screen [S2]
Differs from terminal: this is the display's physics (glow, lines, flicker) and can wrap any content, not only a command line [inferred]
fits: Game interfaces, title screens, retro-tech landing pages, event sites and music visuals.
goes_wrong: Blur and scanlines over long body text make it tiring to read; it works for headlines and short bursts.
accessibility: Glow and scanlines lower legibility; keep core text crisp at 4.5:1, put effects on a decorative layer, and remove flicker under reduced motion.

sources.supports: Monochrome CRTs of the 1960s to 1980s; P1 green, P3 amber, P4 page white; amber seen as easier on the eyes
CSS-Tricks: radial gradient green glow, text-shadow 0 0 5px for blur, repeating 1px/2px gradient for monitor lines
Terminal emulator that mimics old cathode tube screens, with default amber and green profiles

examples.name: cool-retro-term
examples.what: A terminal emulator styled like an old amber or green cathode screen

name: Financial terminal (dense trading screen)
plain: Packed tables of amber numbers on black, built for experts.
origin: Market data terminals; the Bloomberg Terminal has worked this way since 1982 [S1]
defining: Amber characters on black by default, a scheme from early computing [S1]
Screens dense with text, mostly tables, with charts where useful [S1]
Multi-monitor setups and a dedicated keyboard with keys such as EQUITY, GOVT and NEWS [S1][S3]
Yellow and orange text on black that outsiders find ugly but experts are proud to master [S2]
Change is slow: loyal users notice even a slightly changed font [S1]
fits: Trading and analytics tools, operations consoles, observability and power-user dashboards.
goes_wrong: Density without hierarchy: when everything is amber and tight, nothing stands out and newcomers are lost [S2].
accessibility: Amber on black passes contrast, but red and green price moves fail for colour-blind users; add arrows or signs, use tabular figures, and allow zoom without breaking the grid.

sources.supports: Fast Company 2015 (archived): as in 1982, screens dense with tabular text and charts, amber characters on black by default, custom keyboard, users notice small font changes
UX Magazine 2010: black background with yellow and orange text; users take pride in the complex interface
Core77 2013: two-, four- or six-monitor terminal setups

name: Braun functionalism (Dieter Rams)
plain: Quiet white, grey or black panels with one bright colour-coded button.
origin: Braun, Kronberg, Germany, products from the late 1950s to the 1980s; Rams wrote his ten principles in the late 1970s [S1][S3]
defining: Neutral, restrained bodies so the product leaves room for its user [S1]
Colour only to explain function: on the 1987 ET66 calculator numbers are black, operators brown and the equals key yellow [S2][S3]
Round, slightly convex buttons on a strict grid [S3]
As little design as possible: nothing decorative [S1]
On screen: flat neutral panels, circular controls and a single warm accent for the main action [inferred]
fits: Calculators and utilities, audio and hardware companion apps, settings screens and calm product sites.
goes_wrong: Copying the surface (dots and one orange key) without the discipline, so colour becomes decoration instead of meaning.
accessibility: Colour-coded keys must also differ by label or position; keep control edges at 3:1 on grey bodies and labels at 4.5:1.

sources.supports: Vitsoe: Rams's ten principles from the late 1970s; neutral and restrained, as little design as possible; Braun products from 1958 onward
V&A: ET66 calculator, 1987, Rams and Lubs; black number buttons, brown operator buttons, yellow equals
Museum Angewandte Kunst: ET 66, Kronberg, 1987; colour-coded buttons as the interface; convex buttons

examples.name: Braun ET66 calculator
examples.what: Black body with round, colour-coded buttons and a yellow equals key

name: Synth hardware panel (Teenage Engineering-style)
plain: Metal gadget panel with four bright knobs and a tiny playful screen.
origin: Teenage Engineering's OP-1 synthesizer, prototype shown in 2010 and released in 2011 [S2]
defining: A brushed aluminium slab with keys, buttons and a small colour display [S1]
Four colour-coded rotary knobs; the screen shows each knob's effect in the matching colour [S1]
Screen graphics are playful characters and geometric motifs, one per mode, recalling early 8-bit game art [S1]
A 320 x 160 px OLED screen; the makers call limits the product's biggest feature [S2]
On screen: light grey panel, black display window, small labels and a few saturated control colours [inferred]
fits: Music and audio apps, creative tools, hardware companion apps and playful product launches.
goes_wrong: Mystery controls: colour-coded knobs that change jobs raise the learning curve unless the screen labels them.
accessibility: Do not rely on knob colour alone; label every control, keep small labels at 12px or more and 4.5:1, and let animated screen characters pause.

sources.supports: Metropolis: brushed aluminium case, small colour display, four coloured knobs with a colour-coded display, mode graphics recalling early Nintendo 8-bit characters
OP-1 shown 2010, released 2011, 320 x 160 OLED display with mode graphics, limitations as its biggest feature

name: Sci-fi FUI / HUD
plain: Glowing blue lines, rings and readouts like a movie spaceship screen.
origin: Interfaces designed for film, TV and games, now a named craft: FUI [S1]
defining: Mostly blue or cyan on dark; one FUI designer says primaries survive bright set lighting best [S2]
Often one hue per screen (all orange or all blue), made to be glanced at rather than read [S3]
Busy data readouts and fake widgets ('fuidgets'), drawn in thin lines, rings and brackets [S3][inferred]
Animated build-ins and sound effects are part of the interface [S4]
Mixes film storytelling, motion graphics and UI design [S1]
fits: Game interfaces, launch and keynote visuals, space and deep-tech marketing, data-art installations.
goes_wrong: Decoration over data: screens built to look busy on camera become unreadable when people must actually use them [S3].
accessibility: Thin glowing cyan text on near-black blurs; use regular weight or heavier, keep 4.5:1, limit motion and sound, and respect reduced motion.

sources.supports: HUDS+GUIS book page: FUI (Fictional User Interfaces) mixes film, storytelling, motion graphics, UX and UI
Mark Coleran, FUI designer: why blue dominates film interfaces; set lighting washes out screens, primaries look stronger
Christopher Noessel: screens strictly orange or strictly blue, meant to be seen not read; fuidget-filled screens
Arwes: web framework for futuristic sci-fi designs, animations and sound effects

examples.name: Arwes
examples.what: An open-source web framework for sci-fi interfaces with animated frames and sounds

name: Palm OS / early PDA
plain: Tiny black-and-white pocket screen with rounded text buttons.
origin: Palm Computing handheld organisers; the first devices had 160 x 160 px screens [S1]
defining: 160 x 160 px screen at 1 bit per pixel until Palm OS 3.0 added 2-bit grey [S1]
Buttons are text centred in a rounded rectangle; pressing inverts it to white on black [S1]
Full-screen forms; dialogs span the screen width and sit at the bottom [S1]
Built on the 80/20 rule: the most common tasks one tap away, the rest tucked out of sight [S2]
Differs from classic-mac-1bit: one full-screen form per task with stylus-sized buttons, no overlapping windows [inferred]
fits: To-do and notes apps, utilities, watch and other small-screen UIs, retro mobile tributes.
goes_wrong: Shrinking a modern app into a fake tiny screen; the point is fewer features, not smaller pixels.
accessibility: Inverted selection is clear but tiny bitmap type is not; set text at 16px or more, keep targets at least 24px and label icon buttons.

sources.supports: Palm OS Programmer's Companion: 160x160 LCD, 1 bit per pixel until OS 3.0, rounded-rectangle buttons that invert, full-width dialogs at the bottom
Zen of Palm (PalmSource): apply the 80/20 rule, focus on what users do 80 percent of the time

name: Console channel menu (Wii era)
plain: A calm grid of TV-like panes you point at.
origin: Nintendo Wii Menu, 2006, modelled on rows of TVs in an electronics shop [S1][S2]
defining: Rows of equal panes, each one a 'channel', like TVs lined up in a shop [S1]
Pages of 4 x 3 panes, 48 slots in all, with the time and date always on screen [S2]
Games sit beside news and weather at the same size so non-gamers feel welcome [S1]
Navigated by pointing with the remote [S2]
White and pale grey rounded panes with soft blue accents [inferred]
fits: TV and set-top apps, kiosks, family and kids products, launchers and home screens.
goes_wrong: Equal panes make everything equally important, so the key action drowns.
accessibility: Pale panes on white need 3:1 edges; focus must be visible from across a room, so use thick outlines and large type for viewing at a distance.

sources.supports: Iwata Asks (Nintendo): menu of panes inspired by rows of TVs in an electronics shop; the word Channel; panes treated equally
Wii Menu, first released November 2006: four pages of 4x3 grids, 48 slots, time and date, pointer navigation
